description: We are The Goodmartian Labs, a small team from Tajikistan led by a full-stack developer
summary:
Count the fires that NASA satellites saw in 2011 and in 2012, and the world seems to burn six times more. It does not: the jump comes from a change of sensor. The record switched from the MODIS sensor to the sharper VIIRS sensor, and VIIRS sees many more small fires.

Verner joins the two records into one. It converts MODIS counts to the VIIRS scale and builds a monthly burning calendar from November 2000 to the latest complete day for any country, region or area you draw on the map. It covers 275 million detections in 258 countries and 4,596 regions. After the conversion, the 2012 jump is 1.05 times instead of 6.04.

Each month is colored against the same month in earlier years, with the expected error of that area next to it. On years the model never saw, the median error is 8.6 to 10.2 percent. All 12 known fire seasons we listed before the test show up, from Portugal in 2003 to Quebec in 2023. Five of the 12 are from the MODIS years, so the converted past holds up too.

Verner also has an assistant built on the Claude API. Ask it whether June 2023 was unusual in Quebec. It reads the calendar and answers: 131 times the usual June, the highest of 23 Junes. Every figure it says is checked against Verner's data. Ask where a crew could enter a live fire, and it builds a draft work plan.

A fire season of 2005 and one of 2025 can now be compared on one scale.
details:
Verner is built by Goodmartian Labs for the challenge "Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots". Verner is named after Verner E. Suomi, the father of satellite meteorology, after whom the Suomi NPP satellite is named.

What it does. You pick a country or a region, or draw an area on the map. Verner shows a calendar of burning activity for every month since November 2000. Each month is colored against the median of the same calendar month in earlier years (from 2003), and the expected error of the area is shown next to it. You can download hot spots and monthly tables as CSV.

The assistant. Verner has a built-in assistant on the Claude API (Anthropic). You ask in your own language. Ask whether June 2023 was unusual in Quebec, and it checks the calendar and answers that the month had 131 times the usual June, the highest of 23 Junes, with the chart under the answer. Ask where a crew could enter a live fire, and it builds a draft plan with entry points, trail times and a way out. It does not answer from memory. It calls Verner's own tools, which read the same data as the screens. The tools cover four jobs. They find an area and read its calendar. They compare periods and check if a month was unusual, with the ERA5 weather next to it. They list live fires and build a draft crew plan on the map. They draw on the map and save a CSV file or a short report. Each answer comes with a card: a chart, a fire, a plan on a small map or a file to download. Every figure in an answer is checked against what the tools returned. If a figure cannot be traced, the assistant writes the answer again once. If it still fails, you see a notice instead of the answer. When someone describes a fire that threatens them, it only tells them to call the local emergency number.

The problem. NASA has two long fire records. MODIS on Terra and Aqua gives us November 2000 onward at 1 km. VIIRS on Suomi NPP gives us 2012 onward at 375 m. VIIRS sees far more small fires, so the two cannot simply be joined. If you do, the world count of 2012 is 6.04 times that of 2011. With Verner it is 1.05 times.

How it works. A pipeline reads the NASA FIRMS archives for November 2000 to 2025 and the FIRMS API for 2026. It drops low confidence detections, volcanoes and other static sources. For each date it takes one satellite from a fixed chain: MODIS Terra until July 2002, MODIS Aqua until January 2012, VIIRS S-NPP until 1 November 2026 and VIIRS NOAA-20 from 2 November 2026, with the other satellites of the chain as backups. Then it fits conversion factors that turn MODIS counts into S-NPP counts, for each biome and calendar month. A country gets its own factor only when it clearly beats the zone factor. 41 of 50 candidate countries did. We wrote the selection rules before the calculation and did not change them after it.

How we checked it. We ran two tests against S-NPP counts, using the median of 24 zones. In the first, each year of 2012 to 2019 is left out of the fit in turn. Error falls from 84.6 percent without conversion to 8.6 percent with it. In the second, we fit on 2012 to 2019 and test blind on 2020 and 2021. Error falls from 85.0 to 10.2 percent. The bridge from NOAA-20 to S-NPP has a median zone error of 2.6 percent. We also wrote a list of 12 known fire seasons before the run, from Portugal 2003 to Quebec 2023. All 12 are found.

The site shows the expected error for the area you pick. It is 3.4 percent for the world, 9.5 for Argentina and 10.2 for Kazakhstan. For Tajikistan it is 45.5 percent. Small areas have fewer detections, so the band is wide. The site shows that number.

What else it has. Verner lists the fires of the last three complete days, named by the nearest place and with an estimated area. It has a six month outlook. Where a model beats the median of earlier years by at least 10 percent in its own check, the outlook uses the model. Elsewhere it uses the median of the same calendar month. The outlook uses no weather. Wind and weather on the map come from the NOAA GFS grid.

Limits. Values before 2012 are estimates on the VIIRS scale, not measurements. Active fire detections are not burned area. A work plan is an estimate: the decision is made on the spot.

Tools. Python, FastAPI, polars, numpy, scipy, shapely, Postgres, React, MapLibre GL JS. Source code: https://github.com/goodmartian/verner

Use of SI. The code, tests and project texts were written with Claude Code (Anthropic). The in-app assistant runs on the Claude API.
dataRefs: NASA FIRMS: MODIS Terra and Aqua and VIIRS 375 m (S-NPP, NOAA-20) active fire archives, November 2000 to 2025
NASA FIRMS area API: 2026 detections, standard and near real time
NASA Earthdata: FIRMS and the MODIS / VIIRS active fire products behind it
projectRefs: NOAA GFS 0.25 degree forecasts (weather and wind), NOAA open data
Natural Earth: country and region borders (public domain)
RESOLVE Ecoregions 2017: biomes (CC BY 4.0, Dinerstein et al. 2017)
GeoNames cities1000: names of the nearest places (CC BY 4.0)
OpenStreetMap and Overpass: roads, places, fire stations (ODbL)
OpenFreeMap: vector map tiles and style (MIT, data ODbL)
OSRM demo server: driving routes to fires
Copernicus Climate Data Store, ERA5 monthly climate grid (temperature, precipitation)
Esri World Imagery and Reference labels, satellite base map
Google Places API and Routes API, fallback for nearest fire stations and driving routes when OpenStreetMap and OSRM do not answer
Wikipedia, pages of known wildfire events (CC BY-SA)
